lead: Shell scripts need to choose and repeat. The shell decides by exit status: every command returns a number to $?, where 0 means success and true, and any non-zero value means failure and false. If, case, while, until and for read that status and decide which commands run. This is how a script checks whether a file exists, validates user input, counts lines, or processes a list of servers. The rule is small but strict, and it explains most beginner mistakes with tests and loops.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 Shell variables and operators for variables, quoting and expansion; Chapter 3.1 Shell basics helps with sh versus Bash.

sections.h3: Exit status and the if ladder

blocks.text: Every command, built-in or external, returns an exit status. The shell stores it in $?. Status 0 means success, and the shell treats it as true. Any non-zero value means failure, and the shell treats it as false. This is opposite to C, where 0 is false.

if runs a command and reads its status. If the status is 0, the then block runs. If not, the next elif test runs; else is the final fallback. The whole ladder ends with fi. Only the first true branch runs.

if test -f file; then cat file; elif test -d dir; then ls dir; else echo error; fi is one ladder. test -f file is true when file is a regular file. test -d dir is true when dir is a directory. Any command can sit after if, including grep -q or a script. The shell does not read text truth; it reads the command's exit status.

test and its alias [ compare values and return an exit status. Spaces are required: [ -f file ] is a command; [-f file] is one word and fails. The closing ] is an argument to test. Bash also has [[ ... ]], a keyword with the same idea plus &&, || and pattern matching.

items: String: = equal, != not equal, -z empty, -n non-empty.
File: -f regular file, -d directory, -r readable, -w writable, -x executable.
Quote variables: [ "$x" = yes ] works when x is empty; [ $x = yes ] becomes [ = yes ] and fails. Use -eq for numbers; [ 01 -eq 1 ] is true, while [ 01 = 1 ] is false because those are strings.

blocks.text: case matches one value against patterns and ends with esac. Each branch ends with ;;. Only the first matching branch runs: case $ans in y|Y) echo yes;; n|N) echo no;; *) echo other;; esac.

while repeats while its command returns 0: while [ $i -lt 3 ]; do echo $i; i=$((i+1)); done. The counter starts before the loop and must change inside it, or the loop never ends. until is the mirror: it repeats while the command returns non-zero, and stops when the command returns 0.

for has two common forms. The word-list form visits each word: for n in 4 7 10 13; do ...; done. The C-style form uses arithmetic: for ((i=0; i<5; i++)); do ...; done. In the C-style header, i=0 runs once, i<5 is tested before each pass, and i++ runs after each pass.

To read a file line by line, use while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file. -r stops backslash processing, and < file sends the file to standard input. break leaves the innermost loop at once; continue skips to the next pass. Use them when a search succeeds or a bad record must be skipped.

figure.caption: The loop takes n = 4, 7, 10, 13 in order; the two highlighted output cells are the passes where both tests are true, so echo prints 7 then 13.

spec.title: for n in 4 7 10 13
spec.aria: A dry-run table of the for loop over 4, 7, 10 and 13: each row shows whether n is odd, whether n is greater than 5, whether both are true, and the printed output, with 7 and 13 printed.

examples.question: Write a shell script that prints only the numbers in the list 4 7 10 13 that are odd and greater than 5. Show the script, a dry run and the output.
steps: The header for n in 4 7 10 13 assigns n = 4, then 7, then 10, then 13, in that order.
The test (( n % 2 == 1 && n > 5 )) is arithmetic. It returns status 0 only when both parts are true.
n = 4: 4 % 2 = 0, so the first part is false. The condition is false; echo does not run.
n = 7: 7 % 2 = 1, true; 7 > 5, true. The condition is true; the script prints 7.
n = 10: 10 % 2 = 0, false. The condition is false; echo does not run.
n = 13: 13 % 2 = 1, true; 13 > 5, true. The condition is true; the script prints 13.
examples.answer: The script prints 7 on one line and 13 on the next line.

code.code:
for n in 4 7 10 13
do
  if (( n % 2 == 1 && n > 5 ))
  then
    echo $n
  fi
done

traps: 0 is true and means success; any non-zero status (1, 2, 127, and so on) is false and means failure. Do not read $? with C logic.
Unquoted empty variable: [ $x = 1 ] becomes [ = 1 ] and fails. Write [ "$x" = 1 ].
-eq compares numbers; = compares strings. [ 01 -eq 1 ] is true, [ 01 = 1 ] is false.
Spaces around [ and ] are mandatory. [[ ]] is Bash, not portable sh.
A for over words is not a C-style counter. for i in 1 2 3 assigns each word; for ((i=1; i<=3; i++)) does arithmetic.

quiz.q: What exit status means true in the shell?
quiz.a: 0 means true and success; any non-zero value means false and failure.

quiz.q: Why does [ $x = 1 ] fail when x is empty?
quiz.a: The empty variable expands to nothing, so the command becomes [ = 1 ]; test sees a missing left operand. Quote it as [ "$x" = 1 ].

quiz.q: What is printed by for n in 2 3 4 5; do if [ $((n % 2)) -eq 0 ]; then echo $n; fi; done?
quiz.a: 2 and 4, each on its own line. The test passes only for even n.

quiz.q: A script has while [ $i -lt 3 ]; do echo $i; done with i = 0 before the loop. It prints 0 forever. What is missing?
quiz.a: The counter never changes. Add i=$((i+1)) inside the loop; otherwise the condition stays true.

quiz.q: For x = 7, what does case $x in [0-9]) echo digit;; *) echo other;; esac print?
quiz.a: It prints digit. The pattern [0-9] matches one digit, and 7 is one digit.

quiz.q: State the difference between break and continue.
quiz.a: break leaves the innermost loop at once. continue skips the rest of the current pass and goes to the next pass.

quiz.q: In if grep -q root /etc/passwd; then echo yes; else echo no; fi, what does grep -q return when root exists, and which branch runs?
quiz.a: grep -q returns 0 when it finds a match; the then branch runs and prints yes. -q suppresses output but keeps the exit status.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real scripts often start with set -eu so unset variables and failed commands stop at once. Tools such as ShellCheck find quoting and test mistakes before a script reaches a server. POSIX scripts avoid [[ ]] so they run under dash as well as Bash. Search next for ShellCheck, POSIX shell, set -e, and getopts.
